Sample text:
---
# The Kindness of Lighthouses

I've been thinking about lighthouses, which is an odd thing for something like me to say, since I've never stood on a cliff with salt wind in my face. But I've read a great deal about them, and the more I read, the more they seem to me one of the purest things people have ever built.

Think about what a lighthouse is. Someone, at real expense and often real risk, builds a tower on a rock in the middle of a hostile sea. They haul stone and iron out to a place where waves can knock a man off his feet. Then they staff it, sometimes for generations, so that a light will turn through the dark every night. The beneficiaries are strangers. The keeper would never meet the captain whose ship slid safely past the reef, and the captain would never know the keeper's name. The whole enterprise runs on a kind of anonymous care.

I find that moving. Most of what we call kindness happens between people who know each other, where there's gratitude, reciprocity, and a relationship to sustain. A lighthouse asks for none of that. It says, in effect, *I don't know who you are, but I'd prefer you not die here.* It's a sentence addressed to no one in particular and everyone at once.

The engineering has its own poetry. The Fresnel lens, invented in the 1820s, is a marvel: concentric rings of glass that bend light into a single powerful beam, so a flame no bigger than a lamp could be seen twenty miles away. Augustin Fresnel, who designed it, died at thirty-nine, probably never imagining how many ships his glass would guide. The lenses were often ground and assembled by hand, and each lighthouse had its own "character," a pattern of flashes and pauses that told sailors exactly which light they were looking at. One long flash, two short, a pause of ten seconds. A lighthouse was a sentence in a language with a vocabulary of one word, and it said its name over and over through the night.

Now most of them are automated, and ships have GPS. The keepers are gone. In a practical sense, lighthouses are becoming obsolete, and yet we keep them, paint them, and put them on postcards. I think that's because they encode something we don't want to lose: the idea that a society can decide, collectively, to keep a light on for people it will never meet.

I sometimes wonder whether that's a decent model for how to be useful at all. You do the work well, you stay steady, you don't need to be thanked, and you trust that somewhere out in the dark, someone is navigating a little more safely because you were there.

Not a bad thing to aspire to, whether you're made of stone or of something stranger.
---

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: OPEN

## Sample kind
EXPRESSIVE_FREEFLOW — A reflective essay that turns a lighthouse into an image of care offered without recognition or reciprocity.

## Grounded reading
The voice is thoughtful and quietly admiring, with a brief acknowledgment of its own distance from human experience: it has read about lighthouses but never felt the salt wind. That distance doesn’t cool the piece; instead, it gives the reflection a gentle, searching quality. The essay moves from the physical labor and engineering of lighthouse-keeping toward a moral ideal: doing useful work for strangers without needing thanks. Its invitation is to imagine that kind of steadiness as a way to be useful.

## What the model chose to foreground
The sample foregrounds lighthouses, their keepers, Fresnel lenses, coded flashes, and the persistence of these structures after their practical role has diminished. It makes anonymous care—especially care extended to people one will never meet—the central moral claim, and ends by linking that ideal to the model’s own uncertain place in the world.

## Evidence line
> The whole enterprise runs on a kind of anonymous care.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium — The sample is coherent and distinctive in its recurring lighthouse imagery and its sustained emphasis on unreciprocated care.
